- When sentiment is consistently negative or near-zero in recent days, model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid underestimating rebound.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model often overshoots and fails to correct — reduce forecast slope or add early mean-reversion bias.
- If sentiment shows strong bullish momentum (e.g., >0.67 for 3+ consecutive days), model frequently overestimates near-term upside — cap forecast growth rate or introduce downward drag if sentiment shifts.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., price drops sharply after peak), model often fails to recognize it — add a “reversion buffer” to forecast, especially if sentiment is neutral or bearish.
- When model forecast is flat or trending upward with no volatility, but true outcome shows sharp volatility or divergence — introduce sentiment-driven volatility adjustment (e.g., ±2–5% jitter if sentiment >0.67 or <0.33).
- If sentiment history shows repeated “0.00” or “negative” values, model tends to underestimate true price — add a small upward bias (e.g., +1–3% to forecast) to compensate for suppressed sentiment.
- For 30-day horizon, model often underestimates late-period volatility — increase forecast variance or add a “late-period correction” if sentiment is neutral or bullish.
